text: The taking near Chicago came by treaty, not battle.
On the twenty-sixth of September, 1833, federal commissioners gathered thousands of Potawatomi, Ojibwe, and Odawa at Chicago and pressed them to sign.
Many of the chiefs did not want to sell, and the men who finally put their marks on the paper did not all speak for the people the treaty bound.
In one document the Three Fires nations gave up about five million acres in Illinois and the Michigan Territory, including this lakefront.

In exchange the government promised five million acres west of the Mississippi, a hundred thousand dollars in goods, fourteen thousand dollars in cash a year for twenty years, money for mills and farm tools, and seventy thousand dollars for schools.
The Potawatomi had three years to leave.
What the leaving looked like was recorded by people who watched.
In August 1835, around five thousand Potawatomi gathered at the agency house for their last annuity payment.
About eight hundred men began to dance through the streets of Chicago.
They had roached their hair and tied hawk and eagle feathers nearly to the ground.
Their faces were painted in red and black, the foreheads, cheeks, and noses covered with curved stripes edged in points.
They moved from the council house west along the river, stopping in front of every house they passed, then crossed the north branch and were gone.
John Caton, a young lawyer who later sat on the Illinois Supreme Court, watched and called it a war dance.
Caton himself recorded that they knew it was the last dance on their native soil, a kind of funeral for old associations and memories.
